quote: The only thing you need to focus on with market structure is just basic highs and lows. ... Highs, lows is how I identify direction. ... It's how I find areas of interest and entries.
interpretation: Swing highs/lows are the single primitive of the whole method: direction, AOIs, entries, stops and targets all derive from them. No pivot rule is given here; highs/lows are read by eye.

quote: It is based on the sequence of price highs and lows over time and helps traders identify the prevailing conditions of a market, whether bullish, bearish, or ranging. | Key Components of Market Structure: 1. Higher Highs (HH) and Higher Lows (HL): a. Indicates an uptrend where prices are consistently creating new peaks and higher troughs. 2. Lower Highs (LH) and Lower Lows (LL): a. Indicates a downtrend where prices are consistently forming lower peaks and troughs. 3. Break of Structure (BOS): a. Happens when the price breaks a significant previous high or low, signaling a potential trend reversal or continuation.
interpretation: On-screen definitions: uptrend = HH+HL, downtrend = LH+LL, BOS = price breaks a 'significant' previous high/low. 'Significant' is not defined, so this does not supply a pivot rule (OQ-01 stays open). Generic textbook slide, not author-specific wording.

quote: SWING occurs when price breaks an old High or Low | MS is BEARISH | MS is BULLISH | HH - Higher High | HL - Higher Low | LH - Lower High | LL - Lower Low | SFP - Swing Failure Pattern | EH EL | Consolidation / Ranging (No Trend)
interpretation: The only explicit swing statement in Phase 1: a swing 'occurs when price breaks an old high or low', i.e. a swing is confirmed by a break of a prior extreme, not by an N-bar pivot. Supports a break-confirmed zig-zag (OQ-01 interpretation B) over fixed fractal pivots, but gives no size/scale parameter. The 'EH/EL' labels on the ranging diagram read as equal highs / equal lows (inference; not expanded on screen): ranging = highs and lows that neither rise nor fall. Third-party diagram, not narrated as a rule.

quote: Direction can be defined by those highs and lows again as I said. So in uptrend you'd just be making higher highs and higher lows. You'd be breaking highs, respecting lows and then a downtrend would be the opposite where you're making lower highs and lower lows.
interpretation: Operational wording of direction: bullish = breaking highs while respecting (not breaking) lows; bearish = breaking lows while respecting highs. Deterministic once swings are defined (OQ-01).

quote: Yes you do have a little bit of break-through structure in between but that's more internal lower time ... because consolidation ranging is still a direction it's just a sideways direction it's not an uptrend it's not a downtrend it's just sideways it's mean reversion
interpretation: Breaks of structure inside a trend are 'internal lower timeframe' and do not change the higher-scale direction. Ranging is treated as a third direction (sideways, mean reverting). Implies swings must be tracked on at least two scales (internal vs external), consistent with EP2-018.

quote: If you want to make it easier on yourself, you can just go into the line chart and look at that make a bit more easier and that's just what you want to focus on
interpretation: Author endorses reading highs/lows from the line chart (close prices) as a simplification. Suggests a close-based swing detector is an acceptable variant of OQ-01 (research parameter: close-based vs high/low-based pivots).

quote: Push Period of Expansion | Pull Period of Contraction | Shift Period of Change | Price is elastic | Just trying to ride the wave | Trend | Range | Trending Range
interpretation: Phases on screen: push = expansion, pull = contraction, shift = change. The adjacent Conditions panel shows only drawn zig-zags labelled Trend, Range and Trending Range, with no percentages or thresholds. Phase 1 gives no numeric condition threshold (OQ-02 numbers still come only from the hourly/15m courses).

quote: a push can be just defined as a period of expansion you're breaking highs if it's bullish breaking lows if it's bearish and you're just making those high highs and high lows that push and expansion
interpretation: Push (expansion) = a sequence that keeps breaking highs (bullish) or lows (bearish). A pull (contraction) is the pullback between pushes. Measurable once swings are defined.

quote: a pullback isn't if it's a when and the bigger the push more likely ... pullback you have a big push up you tend to have a relatively big pullback as well so big push up big pullback ... if you have a massive move up without much pullback likely you're going to have a equal reaction or shift to fill in this move so something always to keep in mind is how you moved previously and looking to like correct previous moves
interpretation: Core premise behind CBR: pullback size scales with push size; a large push without a pullback is expected to be corrected ('equal reaction'). No number given; the 50% target (E1H-037) is not stated here.

quote: and how you shift like how you change from a push to a pull is that you shift ... So in here, we're making higher highs and higher lows. We make a new high and then we break a low and then make a lower high. So that'd be a change of character, a market structure shift.
interpretation: Shift from bullish push to pull: new high, then break of a (higher) low, then a lower high forms. Phase 1 uses 'change of character' and 'market structure shift' interchangeably here, whereas EP1-010 distinguishes CHoCH from type 3. The 'then make a lower high' step suggests the shift is confirmed only after the LH prints (inference).

quote: making buys when low time frame shifts bearish they have a stop loss below previous low they get stopped out and then it goes in their favor it's because you need to wait for market structure low time frame market structure to shift from that pullback to that push so you just want you don't want to enter at like an area of interest a zone you want to wait for that low lower time frame to shift bullish
interpretation: An AOI/zone alone is never an entry: the LTF structure must shift in the trade direction first. Supports 'every entry requires a shift' (E1H-029) and treats AOI as location only (OQ-07).

quote: ideally you always want to be entering around that shift this will give you the the best win rate, the biggest risk towards, you don't want to be entering, you don't really want to be entering late on into the push or early on into the pull. You always want to be entering at that shift or just after that shift.
interpretation: Entry timing relative to structure: at or just after the shift; not late into a push nor early into a pull. Author claims best win rate and R:R (no figures).

quote: here these will be the highs these will be the lows you take out a low and you take out a high take out multiple highs and that will be a shift bullish so you go from making lower highs and lower lows to breaking these highs breaking multiple highs it will pull back and that shifts bullish
interpretation: Bullish shift in a pullback: take out a low, then take out a high (ideally multiple lower highs), then a pullback. Matches type 3 order (low then high for a buy); 'multiple highs' reads as a quality cue, not a count rule.

quote: you can like use basic highs and lows for like a general sort of um area of interest to look for where you're looking for that reaction to as well
interpretation: Prior swing highs/lows also serve as AOIs, not only candle open/close levels. Widens the AOI definition in OQ-07.

quote: Range | Trending Range
interpretation: The conditions slide shows a range as swings bounded by shaded high and low bands, some swings poking beyond the bands. There are no numeric thresholds on screen. It visually supports 'range = highs/lows zones, not single prices'.

quote: So in a trend, you have a lot of push, you still have a bit of a pullback, but it's kind of imbalanced. you're having more push in that pool um and it should be high volume you have big pushes with not not much pullback ... this would be extremely high volume. You're getting lots of breaks to the highs, but not much of a pullback, barely any.
interpretation: Trend = push dominates pull (imbalanced), big pushes with little pullback, many breaks of highs. Qualitative version of E1H-007 (<50% corrections). No threshold in Phase 1.

quote: i really don't like high volume trending conditions because there's no structure for me to like enter at ... I do like trending enough volume for a break not too much that you don't pull back ... But I'm a pullback. I wait for a pullback on this. So I'm going to focus more on this than this. When it's this, I'm not going to trade. When it's this, I'm going to risk more or take more trades.
interpretation: Author as a pullback trader: does not trade high-volume trends (no pullback structure for stop/target), and risks more or trades more in trending conditions with enough volume to break but still pull back. Supports OQ-21 option A for high-volume trend, with a trending range as preferred. The 'this' references are to charts, so which is which relies on context.

quote: The opposite of a high volume trend would be a range. You have an equal amount of a push and a a pool. So it's balanced out. If you're trying to take breakout trades here, you're going to get fucked up. So if you're trying to take buys at highs, sells at lows, you're just going to lose. ... You're just looking to sell at highs, buy at lows.
interpretation: Range = push and pull balanced (equal), i.e. corrections near 100% of the prior move. This fits the 75-100% reading (OQ-02 interpretation A) and conflicts with the '>50% = range' reading (E1H-009). Range trades: sell highs, buy lows, no breakouts.

quote: adapting to conditions is one of the most important skills conditions can also just be identified by that push that pull those highs those lows their balance between that push and that pull
interpretation: The underlying condition metric is the balance between push and pull measured on swings. A correction ratio (pull size / push size) is a faithful operationalisation. Phase 1 gives no averaging rule or window.

quote: this is my favorite condition oh my god a trending range when you have almost equal push and pull but it's like kind of directional with it you're making clear highs and lows the direction is pretty clear but yeah you're having clear pullback clear direction I love trading trading these conditions this is the stuff where I will take three four five trades in a day
interpretation: Trending range = almost equal push and pull but directional (clear HH/HL or LH/LL). 'Almost equal' suggests deeper corrections than the 50-75% band of E1H-007: a possible tension over where the trending-range/range boundary sits. 'Three four five trades in a day' conflicts with the journal slide 'Focus on 1-2 Setups Per Day' (trade_examples) and P2G '1-2 trades/week'.

quote: You can't know if a condition is going to continue. You can only know if it was trending after the trend has like finished or ended. So what you should do, just expect conditions to continue doing what they have been doing. Expect market structure to continue showing you what it has been doing. Don't try to guess that it's going to change. ... If you enter trade and it ranges, look to manage that trade, exit that trade early and adapt to those conditions again.
interpretation: Condition is classified only from completed past structure and assumed to persist (no forecasting). This supports a strictly backward-looking condition window. Adds a management rule: if the condition changes after entry, exit early (links to the time stop E1H-041).

quote: And conditions will happen at certain times. I trade the second hour of Asia because it's pretty much always good enough volume that you have trending conditions, a trending range, a break of structure. Whereas like pre, like the Asia open on gold or the hour before that is going to be like really low volume and a more like ranging. ... I rather just wait for the second hour. So pre-open is kind of ranging.
interpretation: Session-condition link on gold: the hour before the Asia open and the Asia open hour are low volume and ranging; hour 2 of Asia 'pretty much always' has enough volume for trending range / BOS. Author's reason for trading Asia hour 2 (OQ-16). Consistent with P2G-55/P2G-57 (first half of Asia poor).

quote: Connecting Fractals | EXTERNAL VS. INTERNAL STRUCTURE | BOS | EXTERNAL STRUCTURE HIGH/LOW | INTERNAL STRUCTURE HIGH/LOW | MULTI-TIMEFRAME STRONG/WEAK HIGHS & LOWS | = HTF Trend | = MTF Trend | = HTF Structure Points | = MTF Structure Points | = Strong High/Low | = Weak High/Low | Connect Through Shifts • MSS • ChoCh
interpretation: Diagrams show two nested swing scales (HTF and MTF structure points), external vs internal highs/lows, and strong vs weak highs/lows, connected through MSS/CHoCH. There is no rule for which points are external or strong: the slide was not narrated and the terms are only labels on third-party diagrams. Supports a two-scale swing model (OQ-01 interpretation C) but supplies no parameters. Common usage (not stated by Tom) calls a strong high the one that produced a BOS of a low; not adopted.

quote: I don't really think about price through timeframes. I think about price through durations of time. So high timeframe, I would say would be the past week or weeks, maybe sometimes days of price action. So days to weeks would be high timeframe. If this is what the one minute chart, this would be like the past two days of price action so i'd say like that's higher time frame i say the past like eight hours um four to eight hours of price action is like middle time frame and then the past hour to two hours of price action is lower time frame
interpretation: Phase 1 duration tiers: HTF = days to weeks (example ~2 days on the 1m chart); MTF = past 4-8 h; LTF = past 1-2 h. Conflicts with E1H-005 (LTF 30-60 min, MTF 5-12+ h, HTF 1 day+) and EP2-012/EP2-016 (LTF 10-30 min, MTF 4-5 h, HTF past day). Overlaps the 15m course LTF range 1.5-2.5 h (E15-004). OQ-03 now has four tier sets.

quote: A lot of you may have heard about top-down analysis, all that type of stuff. I like top-up analysis because I trade low timeframes. If there's nothing on low timeframes, why would I even bother looking at high timeframes? So I do kind of top up, looking at how low timeframe is and then look for high timeframe to align with that as well.
interpretation: Process order: check the LTF for a setup first, then look for HTF alignment. Consistent with EP2-014 (LTF must be aligned first). For a backtest, the LTF trigger is the gate and HTF context is a qualifier.

quote: the best trades will be like a high time frame continuation with like a low time frame reversal where you have like a shift um and then you could possibly even have like a shift within the shift of an overall continuation those have always been the best trades
interpretation: Highest-quality setup archetype: HTF continuation entered through an LTF reversal (shift), optionally a shift within the shift. Matches journal setup tags 'LTF Reversal' + 'HTF Continuation' (trade_examples slide).

quote: ideally you want to align all three but two tends to be good enough so it could be low time frame with middle time frame low time frame with high time frame if you're trading low time frame you always want ... otherwise you'll enter too early you'll get stopped stopped out and then it will go in your favor
interpretation: Alignment scoring: all three durations ideal; two is enough, and the two must include LTF (LTF+MTF or LTF+HTF). Same as EP2-014 and the journal 'MS Align' count (1-3).

quote: you can take a buy stop below the low and you can kind of ride that up with that high time frame when you align internal structure with external structure you get the highest probability of a win you get the best risk to awards
interpretation: Internal (LTF) structure shifting back in line with external (HTF) structure = highest probability. The stop sits below the LTF low that formed the shift. Author claim, no figures.

quote: you might have a failure to break a high and then you break a low you'd be like now high time frame has shifted bearish change your character on the high time frame and you can align that pullback with a low time frame shift for really nice alignment of a continuation
interpretation: HTF bearish CHoCH = price fails to make a new high (lower high), then breaks a low. Gives a sequence rule usable for an HTF-scale direction flip once swings are defined (OQ-01).

quote: Candles are just simplified market structure | Each HTF candle = a LTF MS range | HH HL LH LL | HTF CANDLE LTF STRUCTURE (1) BULLISH | Candle Behavior is all about giving "Timing" to Structure
interpretation: The diagram labels HH/HL on a bullish candle whose high and low are both above the previous candle's high and low (LH/LL mirror), with dashed lines at the prior extreme. This gives a deterministic candle-to-candle definition of HH/HL on HTF candles. Candidate swing primitive for OQ-01: consecutive candle highs/lows on a chosen timeframe, no N-bar pivot needed. Each HTF candle equals one LTF structure range (body = the LTF range).

quote: if we're expecting they can like if we're expecting it to continue moving bullish and we've had some previous bullish candle closes you expect the new candle to reverse in the first half in relation to how the previous candle closed so if the previous candle closed bullish you expect the new candle open to create a bottom wick burst in that first half and then push bullish in that second half for a continuation
interpretation: Core candle-behavior timing rule: after a bullish close, a continuation candle first retraces (creates its bottom wick) in its first half, then pushes bullish in its second half. Mirror for bearish. 'bottom wick burst' is read as 'bottom wick first'. Deterministic on sub-candle data.

quote: Like when, when do you expect for it to pull back? When a new candle is opening, this could be the alley, the 30 minute, the 15 minute. I expect this to pull back in the first 15 minutes of a 30-minute candle if the previous closed bullish so yeah makes it a lot easier to get that timing always keep in mind where when are you in that previous candle close or in the in the current candle are you in the first half the second half of the alley and this is fractal as well so five minute 30 minute 15 hourly for our daily
interpretation: 'First half' = the first 50% of the candle's duration (30m candle: first 15 min; hourly: first 30 min). The rule applies fractally to 5m, 15m, 30m, hourly, 4h and daily candles ('alley' = hourly, 'for our' = four hour).

quote: ideally for let's say bullish candles if you the strength will be higher if you have a bigger body bigger clothes above price and for bearish it'll be the opposite so with wicks as well the bigger the bottom wick the more it shows that there was a rejection of lows the bigger the top wick the more it shows there was a rejection of highs so for bullish structure or bullish candles want bigger bottom wicks um like smaller top wicks and you can kind of see the strength decreases by the relation of the bodies to the wicks ... how bullish is it how bearish is it just if it closes bullish doesn't mean it's actually going to be bullish
interpretation: Candle strength is graded, not binary: a bullish candle is stronger with a larger body (close far above the open) and a larger bottom wick relative to its top wick. Strength falls as wicks grow relative to the body. No thresholds. Measurable proxies: body/range ratio and (lower wick - upper wick)/range (RESEARCH-DERIVED). Relevant to OQ-08 'decisive'.

quote: Bodies and Wicks | Candle Strength | Wick Size | Body Size | Prev Candle Wicks | Size of candle relative | Opens and Closes | BUYERS IN A FULL CONTROL | SELLERS SHOWED THEIR STRENGHT, BUT BUYERS OUTPERFORMED | INDECISION ON THE MARKET | BUYERS WERE IN CONTROL BUT SELLERS REJECTED THEM | Candle Timing | More volume at opens and closes | LTF direction changes | First and second half
interpretation: Slide lists the candle-strength inputs: wick size, body size, previous candle's wicks, candle size relative to neighbours, and opens/closes. Examples: full-body = full control; long lower wick + body at top = sellers rejected; small body with both wicks = indecision; long upper wick with body at bottom = rejection. The timing panel states more volume at opens and closes, new HTF candle opens are commonly where LTF direction changes, and first vs second half. Still no numeric thresholds.

quote: also no wick candles i've talked about if you immediately open let's just say this is a we've been moving bearish and you immediately open and you just push bearish without creating much of a top wick this shows that price is like moving immediately with volume in a certain direction so we always want to be trading with volume and if i'm looking to take a sell and and there's no bottom wick, that will decrease the probability of it being a good trade or profitable trade because volume is shifting bullish. Ideally, you want it to open, right? Like be a bit indecisive, create a little bit of bottom wick, maybe break a low and then reverse.
interpretation: No-wick candle = opens and pushes immediately with no opposite wick, which shows volume in that direction. Trading against a no-wick candle lowers probability (the speech mixes up top/bottom wick). Preferred: the candle opens indecisively, makes a small opposite wick (maybe breaking a low), then reverses. This sits in tension with the CBR premise that an hour opening and extending without a pullback (minimal opposite wick, E1H-020) is what gets faded, and with VP1-2_2, where an immediate push is a reversal signal. Probably reconciled by timing: don't fade a no-wick push early; the OE fade comes 20-30 min later after a shift. Author claim elsewhere: trading against no-wick candles = 38% (P2G-44).

quote: With candles, especially higher time frame candles, a lot of time they can signal more volume. So when a new high time frame candle opens, there tends to be more like high time frame volume. ... have an hourly open volume increases a 30 minute open there's more volume so i tend to find there's high volume at new high time frame candles
interpretation: Volume/volatility rises at new hourly and 30m candle opens. Suggests time-since-HTF-open as a volume proxy (OQ-08) and underpins the :00/:30 timing anchors.

quote: another thing to keep in mind as well when a new high time from candle opens other time it can signal a shift or a change in direction so especially on a 30 minute i take a lot of trades that are 30 minute reverses ... here candle behavior states that if we're looking for it to continue you're expecting it to create a bottom wick i pull back first and then push if If you push straight away, that can be a really clear signal of it shifting or reversing. ... The periods where it just pushes straight away, or might be a bit incisive than push, in the first half, that can be a signal that it's going to reverse as well. So new 30-minute hourly candles can be changes in direction.
interpretation: If a new candle skips the expected first-half opposite wick and pushes straight away (or hesitates, then pushes) in its first half, expect a reversal around the next sub-candle open (e.g. the 30m mark of the hour). This is the candle-behavior basis of the 30-minute reversal and CBOE. It qualifies VP1-2_1 (don't trade against a no-wick push immediately; do expect it to reverse later).

quote: i take a lot of revert like reversal trades around a 30 minute candle um just like fill in the previous move to correct some of that um especially when you align it with high time frame direction
interpretation: The author's most frequent setup is the '30-minute reversal': a reversal around the 30m open that corrects part of the prior move, best when aligned with HTF direction. Matches the journal 'P.Hour: 30m Reversal' tag and E1H-024 timing.

quote: my what are some of my best trades were ever on like my best trades ever yeah um have been based off four hour candle behavior you create that you have a four hour candle close bearish um i'm kind of expecting it to be bearish ... i enter in the first two hours of that four hour candle in that first half on the top wick being formed it flips pushes bearish and i get like a what one two six one two seven rr trade very rare that i get this
interpretation: 4h application of the same rule: after a bearish 4h close, sell during the first 2 hours (first half) while the top wick forms. Author claim: occasional ~1:26-1:27 R:R outcomes, 'very rare'. Anecdote, not a statistic.

quote: All timeframes show the same thing, just in different amounts of detail | Lower Timeframe = More Detail | Higher Timeframe = Simpler | How I use it: 10 min avg trade duration | Market structure - 1m, 5m, 15m | Candle Behavior - 5m, 15m, 30m, 1h, 4h, D, W | Think about duration of price, not timeframe.
interpretation: Phase 1 version of the EP2-011 slide without the 'L TF: 10-30m | M TF = 4-5h' lines. Market structure is read on the 1m/5m/15m charts, candle behavior on 5m through weekly; average trade ~10 min. Chart timeframes and duration tiers are separate concepts (OQ-03).

quote: i always think about time frames or duration of price i always think about it yeah through duration of price i'm trading in the next 10 minutes not the one minute or the five minute i my the average duration of my trade is around 10 minutes ... for market structure i'm mainly using i'd say mainly the woman and the five minute mainly the one minute and then for counter behavior because each high like the hat the high time frame the candle the bit the larger the duration of price um i might trade like 550 15 minute structure wise um i might just trade like one 30 minute candle one or two maybe three 30 minute candles uh two hourly candles like i might look at how an hourly candle forms in relation to the previous hourly candle close
interpretation: Market structure mainly on the 1m chart ('woman' = one minute), also 5m. Candle behavior uses only the last 1-3 candles of the higher timeframe (e.g. one to three 30m candles, two hourly candles: the current hourly candle vs the previous close). The CB lookback is therefore 1-3 HTF candles, not a long HTF structure.

quote: ideally you want to be using lower lower time frame lower time frames when it's more volatile because if you wait for high time frame to shift it's just going to move without you so low time frames allow you to enter earlier allow you to have a bit more precision
interpretation: Entry timeframe choice depends on volatility: the more volatile the market, the lower the entry chart. Consistent with E15-038 (fast market: breakout on a small shift) and the 5s/1m entry models (OQ-10).

quote: think about duration of price not time frame i rarely care about daily four hour structure because um what is it like daily four hour structure um yeah we have an uptrend but how like long is the uptrend that's like 20 days of price action i'm trading 10 minutes why do i care about daily like four hour structure i'm just trading like individual candles
interpretation: Daily/4h chart structure (weeks of price) is 'rarely' used. The HTF enters through the behaviour of individual recent candles. This limits the HTF alignment tier to roughly days, not weeks; it is in tension with VP1-1_5 'HTF = days to weeks'.

quote: okay sorry let me get this previous alley closed bearish you pull back in that first half you create that top wick in that first half around that 30 minute so in the first 30 minutes sorry um in the first 30 minute you're bullish in the second 30 minute you're bearish you change that direction ... The 30 minute direction shifts at that new 30 minute candle open, what a type three pretty clear type three candle and then you push in that second half of the alley candle for clear direction ... a lot of times you have a continuation on the alley then like pull pullback or reversal around that 30 minute
interpretation: Worked hourly example: previous hour closed bearish; the new hour pulls back bullish in its first 30 min (forming the top wick); at the :30 open the 30m direction flips with a type 3 shift; the second half pushes bearish. The phrase 'the hourly candle flips and moves bullish' (00:05:55) contradicts the rest and reads as a slip. Reversal anchor = the :30 open, earlier than the ~:37 'best' in E1H-024.

quote: this will happen exactly the same way on the daily so if the previous day closes bullish you're expecting to create a bottom work or move bearish at the start of asia or the start of the the day so i used to take a lot of losses um because i tried to trade with high time frame direction ... if you're in the first half of the candle you shouldn't be looking for buys you should be looking for sales to create that bottom week first and then you flip later on in London, New York to move bullish. ... So depending on when you're trading, if you're trading Asia session and the previous day is a bullish close, you likely shouldn't be looking for buys. Okay. You should be looking for sales to create that bottom wick in that first half
interpretation: Daily candle behavior as a session bias: after a bullish daily close, expect Asia (first half of the day) to move bearish and form the daily bottom wick, with the bullish push in London/New York; mirror after a bearish close. For Asia trades this is a directional bias against the prior day's close. Conflicts with E1H-028 ('don't worry about candle behavior day') and the OQ-15 default (daily CB not a filter). VP1-trade_examples shows the nuance: a buy taken after the Asia bottom wick had already formed.

quote: Hourly | Bottom wick created in Asia | Prev close bullish | Bearish Close | Bullish Asia | Bearish Asia | Bullish Close
interpretation: Annotated daily examples: after a bullish previous close, the bottom wick is created in Asia; after a bearish close, Asia is bullish; after a bullish close, Asia is bearish. Supports the daily CB session bias in the preceding record.

quote: weekly exactly the same um you have a previous weekly close monday wednesday you move so monday tuesday wednesday you move bearish you create that bottom wick on the week and then later on in that week wednesday thursday friday you push bullish
interpretation: Weekly candle behavior: after a bullish weekly close, Mon-Wed forms the bottom wick (bearish), Wed-Fri pushes bullish. Consistent with E1H-043 (weekly reversal Tue-Thu).

quote: So first off, we have levels. A level is just a clear formation at a open and close. So when you go from, say, a bearish candle close, so the close is there, and then you have the bullish candle open. When that candle closes, when it closes as a bullish candle, you're going from a bearish to a bullish candle, the open and the close creates a level. So creates a level for price tends to react to that level.
interpretation: Deterministic level rule: a level forms only where candle close direction flips (bearish close followed by a bullish close, or vice versa). The level price is the junction: the prior candle's close and the next candle's open. Narrower than E1H-014 ('hourly candle opens and closes'), which implies every open/close. Partially resolves OQ-07 (level construction).

quote: Areas of Interest | Levels | A new level forms when there is a shift in candle close direction | Zones | General Area around Highs and Lows | Refinement | Refine down to lower timeframe highs and lows | Hourly | 15m | 1m | Entry Relativity | Ideally want to enter in the upper half for sells and lower half for buys | Candle close direction changes in your favor e.g. going from a bullish to a bearish close and vice versa Every type 1 creates a level
interpretation: On-screen AOI pipeline: Levels (formed on a change in candle close direction; every type 1 creates one) -> Zones (general area around LTF highs/lows) -> Refinement (hourly -> 15m -> 1m highs/lows) -> Entry relativity (sells upper half, buys lower half of the previous move). Confirms the level rule and gives the refinement chain.
